tweets.text:
My mother recently died, and one of the last things she said to me was this:

"There was a while there where I was certain you were either gonna kill yourself or become a monk."

She was right. That was where I was at, and it began because my ex aborted our baby.

At the time I was in the military with a steady paycheck. I'd been hoping to marry my girlfriend for years by then, and after she found she was pregnant we started talking about baby names... I called her mother, told her her grandchild and her daughter were safe with me. I was ready to become a father.

Then I got the call, a month or so later: "It is finished." She'd gone and had it killed, disposed of. It was over. Up to that point I'd taken the whole "her body her choice" thing as a given, and I did not react much at first -- but that day a darkness swept over me that brought me to the lowest point of my life. My own flesh and blood was killed in vain; the woman I'd joined the military for had spurned me -- a lifetime of bad decisions hit me like an avalanche, and my baby was gone, chopped up, dead.

I was ready to die. Covid "quarantine" was back in full swing; I was trapped in my barracks room alone. I googled how to pray the Our Father -- a prayer I'd learned as a Catholic choir boy many years before. And I prayed day and night, again and again. I learned to pray the Rosary. Then I learned to pray the Rosary in Latin. I said Memorares for my deceased baby. I constantly prayed to find a way to forgive my ex. Within six months, and after wrestling with serious bouts of alcoholism and suicidal ideation, I'd be a Christian again -- and within a year, I'd receive the true Flesh of Jesus Christ again at a Catholic Church in New Orleans.

That period was insanely dark. It began with an abortion. I learned to be chaste; I went to daily Mass. I told my mother that when my enlistment was over I was going to go with the Franciscans. My ambition was to live a life of penance for my culpability in the murder of my own child.

But just before my enlistment ended, I met my wife. Now she's a week overdue with our first baby! And my mom died four days ago -- I asked her if she'd take care of my other baby in the afterlife. And she (a non-Christian, pro-abortion type woman) said "I will do that. I will absolutely do that" and meant every word.

I can't tell you how much that meant to me. I'll remember it when we're holding our new baby later next week -- bringing that child to Mass, to sleep in the presence of Christ, praying for those we've lost.
